edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SCIENCE & TECH + SPORT
edition.deck: A selection of consequential developments in world affairs, the UK and Denmark.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises major public-affairs, health, environmental and economic stories. Related reporting has been grouped where it adds context; allegations and unsettled claims remain attributed.

content.headline: Ukraine says Russian strikes killed at least 24 across several regions
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine says Russian strikes killed at least 24
content.standfirst: Overnight attacks hit residential areas and energy infrastructure, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky. Rescue workers are searching a destroyed apartment building in Pryluky, where he says 18 people, including four children, died.

image.caption: Damage from overnight Russian strikes in Ukraine.

sources.originalTitle: Zelensky condemns 'vile' large-scale Russian attacks that killed 24

segments.body: At least 24 people were killed in overnight strikes across central and eastern Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said. He reported 18 deaths, including four children, in the destruction of a five-storey apartment building in Pryluky; Ukrainian officials also reported casualties in Dnipro, Kremenchuk, Kyiv and Oleksandriya.

segments.title: Calls for air defences
segments.body: Zelensky said Russia fired 70 missiles and renewed his call for allied air-defence support, saying Ukraine’s forces intercepted only some of them. He said energy infrastructure was among the targets. Moscow had not commented on the latest strikes at the time of the report.

content.headline: Kenya quarantines contacts after its first reported Ebola death
content.shortHeadline: Kenya quarantines contacts after first reported Ebola death
content.standfirst: Authorities are tracing contacts after a man died in Nairobi following travel from DR Congo through Uganda. Health officials are investigating how he crossed several borders and flew to Kenya while reportedly ill.

image.caption: People at an Ebola isolation facility are kept under observation.

sources.originalTitle: Ten people linked to Kenya's first-ever Ebola case quarantined as screening concerns grow

segments.body: Ten people who had contact with the man have been quarantined, and Kenyan authorities are trying to trace 57 others. He died in a Nairobi hospital on Monday after travelling from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda. Kenya says this is its first Ebola case.

segments.title: Questions about screening
segments.body: Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya questioned how the patient travelled through several cities, drove to Uganda and flew to Kenya without his illness being detected. Kenya’s health ministry suggested medication may have masked his symptoms. Officials say they have increased surveillance, while Kaseya said temperature checks alone are unreliable and rapid testing is not available at border points.

content.headline: France suspends stun grenades at protests after teenager loses hand
content.shortHeadline: France suspends stun grenades after teenager loses hand
content.standfirst: The interior minister ordered a pause while investigators establish what happened in Lens. The decision comes amid widening student protests, complaints about police force and conflicting accounts of how the 15-year-old was injured.

image.caption: Protesters demonstrate in Paris during France’s student protests.

sources.originalTitle: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests

segments.body: France has suspended the use of stun grenades to police student protests after a 15-year-old boy lost a hand in Lens. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the pause would remain until the circumstances of Monday’s incident were clarified. Authorities say the boy picked up a grenade before it exploded; students allege an officer fired it directly at him.

segments.title: Protests continue
segments.body: More than 500 schools were fully or partly closed on Wednesday, and hundreds of thousands of people joined demonstrations on Tuesday, according to the report. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 security-force members injured. Police watchdog IGPN has opened 18 investigations into whether officers acted proportionately.

segments.title: A disputed decision
segments.body: A policing union leader questioned the suspension, arguing that removing the weapon could lead to more close-quarters clashes and injuries. Rights groups have complained of disproportionate force against teenagers; the government says investigations are under way.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s account details competing claims over the Lens injury and the police union’s concern that withdrawing stun grenades could increase risks during crowd dispersal.

content.headline: Bolsonaro’s son vows to ‘re-democratise’ Brazil after first-round lead
content.shortHeadline: Bolsonaro’s son vows to ‘re-democratise’ Brazil
content.standfirst: Flávio Bolsonaro goes into the 25 October presidential run-off after leading the first round. His ambiguous pledge to change the constitution has alarmed critics, who warn of an authoritarian turn; he says Brazil needs to return to normal.

image.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro, who is leading into Brazil’s presidential run-off.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Another coup d’état’: fears grow as Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re-democratise’ Brazil
Flávio Bolsonaro’s advance in Brazil’s election is grim jolt for climate campaigners

segments.body: Flávio Bolsonaro, son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, led Brazil’s presidential first round and is due to face incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in a 25 October run-off. He has promised to use a stronger far-right presence in Congress to change the constitution and “re-democratise” the country, without explaining what he means by the phrase.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis focuses on the environmental stakes of the election, arguing that a Bolsonaro victory could weaken protections for the Amazon despite recent reductions in deforestation under Lula.

segments.title: Warnings from opponents
segments.body: Opponents and historians say the language may disguise an effort to weaken democratic institutions. Jair Bolsonaro was jailed for trying to engineer a coup after losing the 2022 election. Flávio Bolsonaro rejected speculation that he intends to complete his father’s project, telling reporters Brazil needs to “go back to normal”.

content.headline: US Republicans balance Trump loyalty against voters’ cost-of-living concerns
content.shortHeadline: Republicans weigh Trump loyalty against cost-of-living anger
content.standfirst: With November’s midterms approaching, Republican candidates are trying to address high prices without breaking with a president who remains dominant in the party. Polls cited by the BBC show widespread dissatisfaction with the economy.

sources.originalTitle: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
Modstanderne lugter blod, men Trump har måske et es i ærmet

segments.body: Republican candidates are confronting a difficult midterm choice: echo Donald Trump’s upbeat account of the economy or acknowledge voters’ concerns about affordability. The BBC cites inflation of 3.4%, rising petrol and record beef prices, as well as polls showing many Americans think the economy is worsening.

perspectives.body: TV 2 reports that Democrats are increasingly optimistic about winning the House and possibly the Senate, while Trump’s vague hints of a coming “surprise” have prompted speculation. Neither Trump nor the White House has explained what he meant.

segments.title: No easy break with Trump
segments.body: Some Republicans, including Florida gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds, are speaking about high costs without mentioning Trump. Others have criticised specific policies, including his immigration crackdown and the Iran conflict. But strategists quoted by the BBC say a public break can look opportunistic, while Trump has shown he may retaliate against dissenters.

content.headline: India opposition MPs protest voter-roll changes; Rahul Gandhi detained
content.shortHeadline: India opposition protests voter-roll revision
content.standfirst: Rahul Gandhi and other opposition MPs were detained during a march demanding the chief election commissioner’s resignation. The commission and governing BJP reject claims that a nationwide voter-roll revision is designed to favour the government.

image.caption: Rahul Gandhi is detained by police during the opposition protest in Delhi.

sources.originalTitle: India's opposition leader dragged on to bus as police break up protest

segments.body: Police broke up a protest by Rahul Gandhi and opposition MPs seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of electoral rolls. Gandhi and his sister Priyanka were detained and later released. The opposition says eligible voters have been excluded to benefit the governing Bharatiya Janata Party; both the BJP and the Election Commission deny the allegation.

segments.title: Dispute over the voter lists
segments.body: The commission says the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters; more than 130 million names have been removed from draft lists, according to the report. Opposition parties have also cited an Indian Express investigation alleging commissioners objected to decisions issued in the commission’s name. The commission says decisions were ultimately unanimous. The Supreme Court has asked the government and commission to respond to a petition on the issue.

content.headline: Russia has not confirmed plague in lab worker’s death as calls for answers grow
content.shortHeadline: Russia has not confirmed plague in lab worker’s death
content.standfirst: Officials say there is no epidemic risk after a researcher died in Siberia, but the cause of death remains unconfirmed. The WHO has called for transparent information-sharing as Russia and the US offer conflicting accounts of requests for details.

image.caption: The worker was employed at a plague research institute in Irkutsk, Siberia.

sources.originalTitle: Trump to speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague. This is what you should know

segments.body: A 28-year-old worker at a plague research centre in Siberia has died, but Russian authorities have not confirmed that she had pneumonic plague. The health watchdog said her pneumonia had an undetermined cause and reported no evidence of infection among most contacts who completed medical observation. Russia says there is no epidemic risk.

perspectives.body: The i Paper cites UK experts who say the risk to the wider UK public is very low and that modern antibiotics can treat plague. They say the patient’s cause of death and how she became ill remain uncertain.

segments.title: Calls for transparency
segments.body: WHO director-general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for timely, complete information to assess public-health risks. The US says it has formally requested more information; the Kremlin spokesperson said he was unaware of such a request and accused media outlets of false reporting. Mongolia has ordered precautionary border surveillance, while saying the current risk is low.

content.headline: Chemistry Nobel recognises work on how molecules become one-sided
content.shortHeadline: Chemistry Nobel honours research on molecular ‘handedness’
content.standfirst: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai were awarded the prize for showing how chemical reactions can produce one preferred version of a molecule. The work matters in drug development, where mirror-image forms can behave differently in the body.

sources.originalTitle: Chemistry Nobel awarded for solving mystery of life's asymmetry

segments.body: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has gone to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan’s Kenso Soai for work on chirality: the “left-” and “right-handed” forms of molecules. Their research showed how reactions can be designed to produce more of a desired form, rather than the roughly equal mixture often made in laboratory reactions.

segments.title: Why the distinction matters
segments.body: Mirror-image molecules can have different biological effects, making the distinction important in medicines. The Nobel committee cited the researchers’ work on how one form can emerge selectively; researchers say it also offers insight into why life uses particular molecular forms. The reporting notes that the body can convert between forms of the thalidomide drug, making that example more complex than a simple split between a useful and a toxic version.

content.headline: Badenoch’s inheritance tax pledge draws criticism as Tories court homeowners
content.shortHeadline: Badenoch’s inheritance tax pledge draws criticism
content.standfirst: The Conservative leader says a future Tory government would abolish inheritance tax on family homes and let couples pass on an extra tax-free sum. Critics say the proposal favours wealthier households; the party says it aims to reward people who save.

image.caption: Kemi Badenoch speaks at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.

sources.originalTitle: Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan
‘All me’: Tory party riding high on Kemi Badenoch’s wave of popularity

segments.body: Kemi Badenoch told the Conservative conference that a future Tory government would abolish inheritance tax on family homes and allow couples to leave an additional £1m tax-free. She said the policy would cut the number of estates paying the tax by more than half, with less than 5% of families currently paying it, and said it would be funded by savings the party has identified.

segments.title: Who benefits?
segments.body: Tax Justice UK, Labour, the TUC and Reform criticised the plan as a tax break for the wealthy. The Guardian’s conference reporting also describes Badenoch’s wider policy programme as focused on affluent voters, while noting that some Conservatives question whether those announcements amount to a coherent election strategy. The Tories say the policy rewards hard work and saving.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that Badenoch’s personal standing at conference appears stronger than the party’s wider profile, while some Conservatives worry her choices and emphasis on tax breaks for wealthier households could leave the party looking like a one-person operation.

content.headline: Canadian Weston family agrees to buy Boots for $8.9bn
content.shortHeadline: Weston family agrees to buy Boots for $8.9bn
content.standfirst: Wittington Investments, controlled by the family behind Canada’s Loblaws and Shoppers Drug Mart, is set to acquire Boots’ UK and Irish stores, No7 and its opticians business. The deal requires regulatory approval and is expected to close in 2027.

image.caption: Boots is part of the Weston family’s planned acquisition of UK and Irish retail businesses.

sources.originalTitle: Canada’s Weston family buys Boots for $8.9bn

segments.body: The Canadian Weston family’s holding company, Wittington Investments, has agreed to buy Boots for $8.9bn (£6.74bn), with backing from investment firm Fairfax. The deal covers the retailer’s UK and Irish operations, its opticians chain and No7 beauty brand. Boots has about 1,800 stores and 50,000 employees, according to the report.

segments.title: A change of ownership
segments.body: The transaction would end Stefano Pessina’s long association with Boots and return the Weston family’s Canadian branch to the UK high street after it sold Selfridges in 2022. The deal is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027. Wittington’s chair says it plans stable ownership and further investment.

content.headline: Forever chemical detected in English rivers and groundwater, tests find
content.shortHeadline: Forever chemical found in English rivers and groundwater
content.standfirst: Environment Agency tests found trifluoroacetic acid at all 50 surface-water sites sampled and 43 of 49 groundwater sites. Scientists say the chemical’s health effects and future levels remain uncertain, and the UK has no limit for it in water.

image.caption: The River Ancholme in Lincolnshire had the highest TFA concentration among the surface waters tested.

sources.originalTitle: Forever chemical linked to fertility issues found in rivers in England

segments.body: Environment Agency tests conducted between March and July 2024 found trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), a persistent chemical in the PFAS group, in all 50 surface-water sites tested and 43 of 49 groundwater sites in England. Some sites are within areas supplying drinking water. The highest surface-water reading was in the River Ancholme in Lincolnshire.

segments.title: Unresolved risks and regulation
segments.body: The European Chemicals Agency has recommended classifying TFA as a presumed reproductive toxicant, based on animal testing; effects on people remain under study. One expert quoted said the measured levels do not necessarily trigger health problems now, but rising concentrations are concerning. England has no TFA limit for drinking water, and the Drinking Water Inspectorate is studying the risks.

content.headline: SEND support plans face staffing concerns and possible delays
content.shortHeadline: SEND support plans face staffing concerns and delays
content.standfirst: A £1.8bn scheme to bring specialists into mainstream schools faces warnings about shortages of therapists and educational psychologists. Separately, sources fear a delay to wider SEND reforms, though the Department for Education says it remains on track.

image.caption: Schools minister Georgia Gould announced the “experts at hand” scheme at Labour conference.

sources.originalTitle: SEND pupils’ extra support at risk with schools unable to access specialist staff
SEND reforms face new delays, insiders fear

segments.body: The government’s “experts at hand” scheme aims to expand mainstream schools’ access to educational psychologists, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and specialist teachers, backed by £1.8bn over three years. At least 36 councils have raised staffing concerns, Schools Week analysis cited by the i Paper found. A specialist charity leader said she had received no firm plans from the councils it works with.

segments.title: A wider reform timetable in doubt
segments.body: Sources quoted by the i Paper said publication of the government’s wider SEND reform response and legislation, expected in November, may slip into the new year after a change of education secretary. The reforms are intended to change eligibility and increase support in mainstream schools. The Department for Education says it is on track and committed to its implementation timetable.

perspectives.body: The i Paper reports uncertainty among government insiders about the legislative timetable, while the Department for Education says it is reviewing consultation responses and remains committed to the planned implementation dates.

segments.title: The delivery challenge
segments.body: School leaders and unions warn that shortages and long waits for specialists could leave families expecting help that is not available. The Department for Education says the programme is phased over three years and that it is investing in recruitment, capacity and training.

content.headline: Nurseries to face proposed limits on staff phones and child photographs
content.shortHeadline: Nurseries to face proposed limits on phones and photos
content.standfirst: New government guidance is expected to restrict personal devices in childcare areas and limit routine photos of each child. The plans follow abuse and data-security cases; staff representatives say training and staffing conditions will also affect safeguarding.

image.caption: Proposed guidance would limit personal devices and photography in childcare settings.

sources.originalTitle: Nursery staff to be banned from using phones after ‘chilling’ child abuse case

segments.body: Government guidance expected this month is set to tell nursery staff, childminders and visitors not to use personal phones or digital devices in childcare areas. Settings would use a designated work device, with safeguards, and generally take no more than one photo of each child per day. Parents would need to give written permission for images.

segments.title: Safeguarding and practical concerns
segments.body: The plans follow the case of a nursery worker jailed for abusing children and a cyberattack involving children’s images and personal details. The proposed guidance also calls for checks of work devices and warns against posting children’s photos on social media or uploading identifiable images to AI tools. A union representative says staff shortages and inconsistent training may make safeguards harder to apply.

content.headline: UK consulate in East Jerusalem to close after Israel’s order
content.shortHeadline: UK consulate in East Jerusalem to close
content.standfirst: Israel ordered the mission to shut after the UK banned trade with illegal settlements and sanctioned people involved in them. The consulate provides services to Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza; the UK embassy in Tel Aviv will remain open.

image.caption: The UK consulate in East Jerusalem is due to close following Israel’s order.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors

segments.body: The UK consulate in East Jerusalem is due to close after Israel ordered it shut in response to the UK’s ban on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and related sanctions. The UK embassy in Tel Aviv remains open. The East Jerusalem consulate provides services to Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza.

segments.title: Impact on Palestinians
segments.body: Amjad Iraqi of the International Crisis Group said Palestinians would bear the cost of the closure, arguing that Israel’s response was aimed at limiting UK support for them. Residents interviewed by the Guardian expressed disappointment at what they saw as a lack of international action. The closure marks a sharp deterioration in UK-Israeli relations, the report says.

content.headline: UK intelligence agencies to review material after German spy chief arrest
content.shortHeadline: UK to review intelligence after German spy chief arrest
content.standfirst: Former BND chief August Hanning is accused in Germany of obtaining classified documents and using them in analysis for a foreign intelligence service. UK experts say agencies will assess whether shared intelligence was exposed; the alleged recipient has not been established in the report.

image.caption: August Hanning led Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service from 1998 to 2005.

sources.originalTitle: The UK security risks after German spy chief arrested, according to experts

segments.body: Britain’s intelligence services are expected to review information shared with Germany after former BND chief August Hanning was arrested on suspicion of espionage. German prosecutors allege that Hanning obtained classified documents, including sensitive assessments and material from partner agencies, and used them in analysis for a foreign service. The allegations have not been proven.

segments.title: What may be at risk
segments.body: Experts quoted by the i Paper say the review will examine whether intelligence could have been compromised, while noting that agencies often remove especially sensitive details before sharing. The investigation has not identified Russia as a current focus, according to the Financial Times as cited in the report; Der Spiegel has reported that Hanning prepared analysis for Azerbaijani intelligence.

content.headline: Dispute over whether schools have new money for teacher pay rise
content.shortHeadline: Schools dispute claim of new money for teacher pay rise
content.standfirst: Education Secretary Lucy Powell says pension-scheme savings mean schools can meet a 3.5% teacher pay award. Unions say those savings were already built into budgets, leaving schools without additional funding and facing cuts elsewhere.

image.caption: Education Secretary Lucy Powell announced the teacher pay award funding approach.

sources.originalTitle: School budgets set to be squeezed to pay for teacher pay rises

segments.body: Education Secretary Lucy Powell says schools can cover a 3.5% teacher pay award through lower employer contributions to local-government pension schemes. The Department for Education says the savings have improved schools’ financial position. Unions and school finance leaders argue the savings were already reflected in budgets and do not amount to new money.

segments.title: Unions seek clarity
segments.body: The NASUWT says schools still face a funding gap and has asked the department to republish details of how the award is funded. A senior Whitehall source told the i Paper the Treasury had not agreed to describe the pension savings as new funding. The department says the award is unchanged and that lower pension costs strengthen schools’ ability to pay for it.

content.headline: Nearly nine million Danish CPR numbers exposed in data leak
content.shortHeadline: Nearly nine million Danish CPR numbers exposed
content.standfirst: The data includes records of people living in Denmark, people who have died and people who moved abroad. Authorities advise organisations not to use CPR numbers alone to verify identity; a teacher whose number was misused describes the lasting consequences of identity fraud.

sources.originalTitle: Det betyder cpr-læk for dig
Folkeskolelærer stemplet som narkoman efter svindel med cpr-nummer

segments.body: A data leak exposed 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers, including records belonging to people who have died or moved abroad. The Agency for Civil Protection and Preparedness recommends that public authorities and businesses use other methods to confirm people’s identities rather than relying on a CPR number alone.

segments.title: Risks beyond the leak
segments.body: A schoolteacher told TV 2 that someone previously used her CPR number to obtain morphine prescriptions, leaving inaccurate drug-use information in her health record and affecting her treatment. A cybersecurity professor said exposed CPR numbers could assist phishing and identity fraud, but cautioned that the leak does not mean everyone’s health records will be misused in the same way.

content.headline: Experts question whether extending Danish North Sea gas licences would improve ‘
content.shortHeadline: Experts question benefit of extending North Sea gas licences
content.standfirst: Greenpeace and Denmark’s Climate Council say continued oil and gas production after 2042 would make little difference to European energy security. The government says it is still assessing economic, climate and energy-independence impacts before deciding whether to start a licensing process.

image.caption: The Tyra gas field in the North Sea returned to production in 2025.

source.credit: Foto: Bo Amstrup / Bo Amstrup / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Ny analyse sår tvivl om effekten af forlænget dansk gasproduktion

segments.body: Greenpeace and the government’s independent Climate Council say extending Danish North Sea oil and gas licences beyond 2042 would contribute little to Danish or European energy security. Greenpeace argues that production would not make the EU self-sufficient and that reducing fossil-fuel use and expanding renewable energy would offer a stronger route to energy independence.

segments.title: Government has not decided
segments.body: Former energy minister Lars Aagaard supports considering an extension, saying even a limited contribution could show solidarity with European neighbours. The current ministry says it has commissioned updated analysis of economic, climate and energy-security effects and will decide after reviewing new information from industry.

content.headline: About 18,000 food-check families may lose home-based student grants
content.shortHeadline: 18,000 food-check families may lose student grants
content.standfirst: CEPOS estimates that about a quarter of the 81,000 young people affected by a proposed cut to grants for students living at home are in families that received a one-off food check. Critics call the policies inconsistent; the prime minister says the change would encourage young people to work.

image.caption: Government ministers presented the food-check measure before the proposed student-grant changes.

sources.originalTitle: Nye tal: 18.000 "økonomisk trængte familier" står til at miste SU til deres børn

segments.body: A CEPOS analysis cited by TV 2 estimates that about 18,000 of the 81,000 young people who could lose student grants under the government’s proposal live in households that recently received a food check. The grant proposal targets students living at home whose parents’ combined income exceeds 710,000 kroner.

segments.title: One-off help and ongoing support
segments.body: Critics from both the left and right say the overlap highlights an inconsistency between describing families as financially strained when awarding the food check and cutting a recurring payment to their children. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has defended the proposed grant change, saying work alongside study can be beneficial. The figures are an estimate from CEPOS, not a government count.

content.headline: Greenland leader says Trump crisis changed Denmark-Greenland relationship
content.shortHeadline: Greenland leader says Trump crisis changed ties with Denmark
content.standfirst: Jens-Frederik Nielsen says the pressure over US demands for Greenland forced closer coordination with Denmark and increased mutual public awareness. He says Greenland still seeks greater self-determination, while describing cooperation as necessary.

image.caption: Greenland’s leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen says the past two years have tested relations with Denmark.

sources.originalTitle: Jens-Frederik Nielsen: Der er noget, jeg gerne vil sige til danskerne

segments.body: Greenland’s leader, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, says the dispute over Donald Trump’s repeated demands for US control of Greenland has changed relations with Denmark. He described January and February as especially tense, saying an invasion could not be ruled out, and said Greenland’s government felt fear among its population.

segments.title: Cooperation and self-determination
segments.body: Nielsen said the crisis required close coordination with Denmark and made more Danes aware of Greenland. He thanked Danish demonstrators and the Danish governments for their support. He also said Greenland continues to seek greater self-determination and should be an equal partner in the relationship.

content.headline: Danish packaging rules may raise household costs despite promised savings
content.shortHeadline: Packaging rules may raise Danish household costs
content.standfirst: Fees have risen in 22 municipalities, and industry representatives say some goods have become more expensive under producer-responsibility rules. Municipal waste companies warn a proposed cap on business payments could leave residents covering more of the costs.

sources.originalTitle: Nye affaldsregler får stik modsat effekt – nu risikerer regningen at blive større

segments.body: A year after Denmark introduced extended producer responsibility for packaging, promised household savings of 500–600 kroner a year have not materialised everywhere. A survey cited by TV 2 found that a typical household’s waste fee rose in 22 municipalities in 2026 compared with 2025. The report also cites businesses that have raised some product prices.

segments.title: Who pays the shortfall?
segments.body: The government has temporarily capped companies’ payments to municipalities and plans a permanent cap. Municipal waste representatives and Local Government Denmark warn that if producers pay less than the full handling cost, residents may face higher fees. A business group says a cap could limit further price rises, while the responsible minister says the system is too administratively burdensome.

content.headline: Kosovo-trained prison officers released after assault allegation in Denmark
content.shortHeadline: Kosovo-trained prison officers released after assault allegation
content.standfirst: Two officers accused of repeatedly punching an inmate at Vestre Prison have been released from custody. The judge found reasonable suspicion but no flight risk; both deny the allegations, and the prison service says it will review their training.

sources.originalTitle: Fængselsbetjente fra Kosovo under oplæring sigtet for at slå indsat i Vestre Fængsel
To voldssigtede fængselsbetjente fra Kosovo er blevet løsladt
Fængselsbetjente fra Kosovo sigtet for vold under oplæring i Danmark

segments.body: Two Kosovo prison officers in Denmark for training have been accused of assaulting an inmate at Vestre Prison. The allegation is that they struck the person repeatedly in the face and body. A judge ordered their release, finding reasonable suspicion but no risk they would flee; both deny the charges.

segments.title: Training programme under review
segments.body: The officers were in Denmark as part of training for work at Gjilan prison in Kosovo, which Denmark plans to rent for people sentenced to deportation. The Danish Prison and Probation Service said it reported the incident to police and would review the training and placement programme. Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said the case was serious.

content.headline: Man jailed for a year over fatal assault at Copenhagen football screening
content.shortHeadline: Man jailed for a year over fatal assault at football screening
content.standfirst: A 31-year-old admitted assaulting a Swedish man at a public screening in Copenhagen; the victim died three days later. The court imposed a one-year sentence for ordinary assault, citing the incident’s circumstances and the defendant’s previous violent convictions.

image.caption: The fatal-assault case was heard at Copenhagen City Court.

sources.originalTitle: 31-årig får et års fængsel i sag om vold ved VM-visning

segments.body: A Copenhagen court sentenced a 31-year-old man to one year in prison for assaulting Christian Zedig, a 32-year-old Swedish police employee, at a football screening at Islands Brygge in June. The man admitted throwing beer cans and punching Zedig, who died on 3 July after an artery was ruptured.

segments.title: Court’s reasoning
segments.body: The court said it took account of the aggressive and escalating conduct, the defendant’s previous convictions for serious offences and the fatal outcome. The sentence was for ordinary assault rather than aggravated assault. Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said some sentences for ordinary violence with fatal consequences are unacceptably low.

content.headline: Denmark expects a high level of flu infections this winter
content.shortHeadline: Denmark expects high flu levels this winter
content.standfirst: The State Serum Institute expects both influenza A and B to circulate, with infections and related hospital admissions potentially reaching high levels. It expects COVID-19 to remain lower; vaccination is offered free to people aged 65 and over.

image.caption: People aged 65 and over are offered free flu and COVID-19 vaccination in Denmark.

sources.originalTitle: Seruminstitut forventer højt niveau af influenzasmitte over vinteren

segments.body: Denmark’s State Serum Institute expects influenza to be widespread this winter, with both influenza A and B circulating and potentially high numbers of infections and related hospital admissions. The institute says influenza B may account for a larger share than in recent seasons, when influenza A predominated.

segments.title: Vaccination and other viruses
segments.body: People aged 65 and over are offered free flu and COVID-19 vaccines, which the institute says provide good protection. COVID-19 is expected to remain at a low-to-medium level. The institute says vaccination of pregnant women against RSV may have contributed to a 70% fall in hospital admissions among infants in the last season, and expects it to reduce illness in young babies again.

content.headline: Victoria Monét makes room for romance on the expansive Frequency of Love
content.shortHeadline: Victoria Monét stretches out on Frequency of Love
content.standfirst: The 22-track follow-up to Jaguar II trades some of Monét’s mischievous confidence for earnest devotion, moving between lush ballads and sounds from different eras. The ambition is compelling, though the long tracklist sometimes blurs together.

sources.originalTitle: Frequency of Love

segments.body: On Frequency of Love, Victoria Monét turns the assurance of her Jaguar albums toward love in its many forms. Swooning ballads, cinematic strings and a slow jam about prioritising pleasure sit alongside the familiar cheek of tracks such as “Head to Toe”. The overall mood is more openly romantic than her earlier work.

The review praises Monét’s range, from the contemporary groove of “Reach Out” to the midcentury echoes of “I Want You”. But across 22 tracks, a similar muted production can make some songs run together, and the guest appearances by SZA and Bruno Mars do not always bring out Monét’s strongest qualities. The album’s scope is part of its appeal and its weakness.

content.headline: Danielle Ponder turns personal upheaval into songs of grief and survival
content.shortHeadline: Danielle Ponder sings through grief and change
content.standfirst: The former public defender left law for music at 40, then faced bereavement, a miscarriage and a painful relationship. On her new album, Everything Has Changed, she turns that upheaval into songs about grief, power and learning to survive.

image.caption: Danielle Ponder, whose new album draws on grief and survival.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Men are a scam!’ The trials of Danielle Ponder, the lawyer turned singer rooting for a better world

segments.body: Danielle Ponder walked away from public-defender work in Rochester five years ago to pursue music full-time. Her debut, Some of Us Are Brave, brought critical attention and placements in television, advertising and games. But as that career gathered pace, her personal life unravelled: her brother-in-law died, her father’s dementia worsened and she had a miscarriage.

segments.title: Making space for grief
segments.body: On Everything Has Changed, the song “Blues” gives stark voice to the miscarriage and the grief that followed. Ponder says shame made it difficult to tell others what had happened; she hopes speaking plainly can help people offer one another care. The songs also reflect on a relationship she describes as a nightmare and on redirecting her energy toward friendships with women.

Ponder’s perspective is shaped by her years as a public defender, when she saw poverty treated as neglect and people imprisoned for minor offences. She connects those experiences to the themes of race and injustice in her music, while her recent videos, filmed in Dakar, express a desire to embody women’s divinity and artistic freedom.

content.headline: Liz Harris finds a restorative kind of connection beyond Grouper
content.shortHeadline: Liz Harris finds a new side of herself with Helen
content.standfirst: The solitary ambient artist’s return to the dream-pop trio Helen brought friendship and collaboration back into focus. A viral hit also exposed how easily streaming platforms can be exploited to steal independent artists’ royalties.

image.caption: Liz Harris, who records as Grouper and performs with the trio Helen.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris is best known for the intimate, often solitary music she makes as Grouper. On Linda’s Head, the second album from her trio Helen, she sings alongside drummer Jed Bindeman and bassist Scott Simmons. Harris says the group lets her show a brighter, more social side of herself, and that rehearsing together helped restore her spirits during medical difficulties.

segments.title: The cost of a viral hit
segments.body: During the pandemic, Grouper’s “Poison Tree” spread widely on TikTok. Harris later learned that someone else had fraudulently registered and uploaded the song, collecting an estimated six figures before she and her label were able to shut down the scam and recover what she was owed. She says fake tracks and remixes continue to make monitoring her work an exhausting task.

content.headline: The Afrobeats label risks flattening Africa’s many pop traditions
content.shortHeadline: Why one label cannot speak for African music
content.standfirst: Artists and critics argue that “Afrobeats” has become a catch-all for sounds across a vast continent. The term has helped African pop travel internationally, but can obscure local traditions and newer styles that need their own names and histories.

image.caption: Tyla, who has argued that African music should not be grouped under one label.

sources.originalTitle: The west has a blinkered view of African music – and it’s hurting the whole continent’s culture

segments.body: Tyla, Tems, Burna Boy and other artists have questioned being grouped under the Afrobeats label, which the article says is now widely applied to African pop, dance, rap, R&B, gospel and more. South African star Tyla, for example, has said she represents amapiano. The label can be useful in marketing, but it does not describe the breadth of the music.

segments.title: What gets lost
segments.body: The article traces how a term that gathered attention around contemporary West African dance music became a much broader category. It argues that this can make emerging sounds harder to document on their own terms: styles such as banku music, azonto and zanku did not gain the same lasting visibility as amapiano. Artists, media and the music industry all have a role in giving new forms context and recognition.

perspectives.body: Culture journalist Tiléwa Kazeem says international publications may treat emerging styles as too “esoteric”, while founder Dolapo Amusat argues that a sound needs documentation, lore and deliberate community-building to stand on its own.

content.headline: Haywire turn hardcore’s rough edges toward melody on I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye
content.shortHeadline: Haywire bring a melodic edge to hardcore
content.standfirst: After a DIY tour through all 50 states helped the Boston band find a wider audience, its second album pairs hardcore’s blunt force with melodic street punk and breakup songs. The shift opens a new door without abandoning the band’s scene-minded roots.

sources.originalTitle: I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye

segments.body: Boston band Haywire built momentum through relentless touring, improvised shows and word of mouth. Their 2025 run across all 50 states helped propel them from local venues to festival slots, a split release with Dropkick Murphys and a deal with Roadrunner. On I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye, the band uses that attention to make a more melodic record.

The album frames a breakup through gruff vocals and catchy, often tender choruses. Songs such as “Trouble in Paradise” and “Perfect Strangers” give the band’s street-punk influences room to shine, while “Flex Your Head” keeps a sharper edge. The closing “Sincerely Yours” offers a tentative note of acceptance before the record ends abruptly, in under 20 minutes.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album keeps protest at the centre
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello turns protest into a solo rock record
content.standfirst: On Everyone Gets What They Want, the Rage Against the Machine guitarist takes the microphone for his first full-length solo rock album. He discusses the political backlash, his late mother’s activism and the people he believes can still change the world.

image.caption: Tom Morello, whose new solo album continues his blend of rock and activism.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes Everyone Gets What They Want as a record for people who have “had enough”. The album combines heavy riffs with songs against racism and authoritarianism, and features Serj Tankian, Kneecap and Morello’s 15-year-old son Roman. Morello says he has never separated music from activism; to him, making art is a form of resistance.

segments.title: A family inheritance
segments.body: Morello says some older Rage Against the Machine fans have attacked his politics, including his support for Covid vaccination. He rejects the idea that the band’s message was ever about individual grievance. His own outlook, he says, came from his mother, Mary Morello, whose activism included opposing racism and supporting workers’ causes. He has established a memorial project encouraging people to act on issues she cared about.

content.headline: Marc Almond says Soft Cell’s final album brings the band’s story full circle
content.shortHeadline: Marc Almond reflects on Soft Cell’s final album
content.standfirst: Soft Cell finished Danceteria shortly before keyboardist Dave Ball died in 2025. Marc Almond recalls the duo’s early rise, their unruly New York years and the sense of closure in releasing one last record together.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball, whose final Soft Cell album was completed shortly before Ball’s death.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Marc Almond says he and Dave Ball agreed that the new Soft Cell songs were finished; Ball died two days later, aged 66. Almond calls Danceteria the duo’s sixth and final album, and says he would not make another Soft Cell record without his bandmate. Its songs revisit the pair’s adventures in early-1980s New York.

segments.title: A scene remembered
segments.body: Almond recalls how two art students who expected to remain an underground act were thrust into pop stardom by “Tainted Love”. New York offered an escape from the pressure to conform, but he also remembers the city’s gay nightlife becoming fearful and desolate as AIDS spread. The album’s celebration of club life is shadowed by loneliness and loss.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul remains a work of productive contradictions
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul still has no single definitive form
content.standfirst: A new deluxe edition revisits the Beatles’ pivotal 1965 album through alternate mixes, outtakes and studio history. The review finds its greatest pleasure not in settling which version is definitive, but in hearing how the record changed along the way.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: The new Rubber Soul special edition includes the UK and US albums, stereo and mono mixes, outtakes and a detailed account of the recording sessions. The review places the record at a turning point for both the Beatles and pop: a meeting point for folk and R&B, art and commerce, and songs that could be intimate yet speak to a generation.

The outtakes reveal a group working under deadline rather than a band inevitably arriving at a masterpiece. Differences between the original national editions, mixes and later remixes reinforce the review’s central point: there is no single “real” Rubber Soul. The new set is a lavish object, but its most rewarding effect is to make a canonical record feel human and still in flux.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning’s mixed reviews expose the limits of Hollywood’s tech scept
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning stumbles over its tech reckoning
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s sequel follows a whistleblower and journalist challenging Facebook’s practices, but two reviews question its dramatic force. Its arrival alongside other films about tech leaders also raises a wider question: can studios meaningfully criticise an industry they are increasingly tied to?

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆
Will the Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman movies make a dent on tech giant evangelism?

segments.body: The Social Reckoning centres on former Facebook employee Frances Haugen and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz as they investigate the company’s impact and its handling of political content. The Guardian’s review finds an entertaining, fast-moving drama, but argues that Mark Zuckerberg is reduced to a near-cameo and that the film avoids naming Trump while discussing the rise of extremist groups.

perspectives.body: The BBC review is more dismissive of the film’s pace and stakes: it says the whistleblower story lacks the tension of a crusading newspaper drama, and that Zuckerberg’s continued power makes a decisive reckoning feel unlikely.

segments.title: A bigger industry question
segments.body: A separate Guardian analysis places the film alongside projects about Elon Musk and Sam Altman, asking whether Hollywood’s new tech criticism signals a united front or simply follows growing public scepticism. It points to the industry’s financial ties to technology companies and warns that marketing buzz is not the same as challenging tech power.

content.headline: Eva Marie Saint, star of North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies at 102
content.shortHeadline: Eva Marie Saint’s screen legacy, from Hitchcock to Kazan
content.standfirst: Saint’s screen career stretched across six decades, from her Oscar-winning role in On the Waterfront to her unforgettable turn as Eve Kendall in North by Northwest. A critical appreciation traces how she brought complexity to the cool blonde persona that made her famous.

image.caption: Eva Marie Saint as Eve Kendall in North by Northwest.

sources.originalTitle: Eva Marie Saint, star of North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies aged 102
Eva Marie Saint: the Hitchcock Blonde who outgrew the persona

segments.body: Eva Marie Saint has died aged 102, a family spokesman said. Her screen debut was opposite Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront, for which she won the supporting-actress Oscar. She later starred opposite Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest and continued acting in film and television for decades, including as Martha Kent in Superman Returns.

segments.title: Beyond the Hitchcock blonde
segments.body: The Guardian’s appreciation argues that Saint’s famous role as the poised, enigmatic Eve Kendall should not obscure the range beneath the image. In North by Northwest, a brief moment of fear and tears punctures her polished appearance; in On the Waterfront and later dramas, Saint brought moral force and emotional restraint to very different characters.

perspectives.body: The appreciation stresses that Saint’s controlled Hitchcock persona was only one part of her career: her work in films such as On the Waterfront and Loving revealed a quieter, more varied subtlety.

content.headline: 24 Hour Party People still captures Tony Wilson’s Manchester world
content.shortHeadline: 24 Hour Party People remains a restless Manchester portrait
content.standfirst: Michael Winterbottom’s 2002 film about Factory Records impresario Tony Wilson returns to cinemas. Its loose, self-aware style can feel formless, but Steve Coogan’s performance suits a media figure who straddled television and the music scene.

image.caption: Steve Coogan as Tony Wilson in 24 Hour Party People.

sources.originalTitle: 24 Hour Party People review – daring metatextual paean to the Manchester music scene

segments.body: Steve Coogan plays Tony Wilson, the television journalist and Factory Records impresario who championed Manchester acts including Joy Division, New Order and Happy Mondays. The film follows Wilson’s promotion of punk and post-punk, his unusual approach to contracts and the eventual collapse of Factory’s business.

The review finds the film’s fourth-wall breaks, real-world cameos and documentary-like touches especially apt for Wilson, a broadcaster who also shaped events beyond the camera. Its baggy, detached energy can make the story feel formless, but the film remains an absorbing, unusual portrait of a music scene and its self-mythologising guide.

content.headline: Artificial turns Sam Altman’s OpenAI story into an uneven tech satire
content.shortHeadline: Artificial’s tech satire is sharp but muddled
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s film casts Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and revisits OpenAI’s early history as comedy and satire. The review admires Garfield’s performance but finds the film’s broad jokes and obvious metaphors blunt its critique.

image.caption: Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever in Artificial.

sources.originalTitle: Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satire

segments.body: Artificial follows Ilya Sutskever’s work on artificial intelligence and his relationship with Sam Altman, played by Andrew Garfield, as OpenAI grows and its leadership tensions sharpen. The film presents Altman as self-interested and manipulative, while contrasting his ambitions with Sutskever’s belief in the technology’s promise.

The review calls Garfield’s performance sharply comic, but says the satire offers limited insight into Altman or the wider culture that welcomes tech leaders. Broad jokes and conspicuous visual metaphors interrupt the film’s more unsettling moments, leaving its warning about AI less focused than its subject demands.

content.headline: James Dean’s East of Eden performance reveals the vulnerable boy behind the icon
content.shortHeadline: The James Dean behind the rebel image
content.standfirst: A close look at East of Eden revisits Dean’s brief career and the intense working relationship with director Elia Kazan that shaped his breakthrough. The film’s most moving moment, the essay argues, is not his cool defiance but his desperate reach for a father’s affection.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean was still an unknown stage actor when Elia Kazan cast him as Cal in East of Eden. The film’s unscripted moments drew on Dean’s own strained relationship with his father, and helped create the restless, unpredictable screen presence that would become inseparable from his image.

The essay argues that the familiar rebel mythology can obscure the vulnerability in Dean’s work. It singles out a scene in which Cal, devastated by his father’s rejection of a birthday gift, reaches out to embrace him. Dean died aged 24, before he could see two of his three leading films released.

content.headline: Digger’s outsize Tom Cruise performance is lost in its own spectacle
content.shortHeadline: Digger is too big for Tom Cruise’s performance
content.standfirst: Tom Cruise plays a wealthy oil baron in prosthetics in Alejandro González Iñárritu’s new satire. The review argues that Cruise’s self-conscious performance overwhelms the film’s quieter moments and its environmental warning.

image.caption: Tom Cruise in prosthetics as the oil baron Digger Rockwell.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Cruise has forgotten how to act

segments.body: In Digger, Tom Cruise plays an ageing oil baron whose company has helped trigger an environmental catastrophe. The i review describes the role as an apparent bid for a transformative, awards-friendly performance, complete with prosthetics, a drawl and an unusually broad physical presence.

The review’s objection is not that Cruise lacks technical skill, but that his image as a meticulous global star remains too visible on screen. Even a scene meant to show private reflection feels like Cruise demonstrating his range. The film’s self-aware performance and publicity make it difficult, the critic argues, to see the character apart from the star.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility makes Austen’s emotional balancing act feel current
content.shortHeadline: Austen’s Sense and Sensibility speaks to the present
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s darker new adaptation follows sisters Elinor and Marianne as they navigate love, money and social expectations. The review finds the film uneven, but sees its central tension—between restraint and romantic impulse—as strikingly familiar.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Georgia Oakley’s Sense and Sensibility.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility

segments.body: In Georgia Oakley’s adaptation, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles play Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, sisters with contrasting temperaments who must face financial insecurity after their family loses its fortune. The film is darker than the familiar 1995 version and, the review says, has a mixed but often compelling approach to Austen’s story.

The review connects the sisters’ different instincts to a modern pressure to balance emotional openness with self-control, and personal fulfilment with the need for security. Marianne’s attraction to Willoughby, whose intentions are “every day implied but never professedly declared”, feels especially recognisable to the critic as a modern situationship.

content.headline: Carrie’s new television adaptation divides critics over its softened heroine
content.shortHeadline: Carrie’s reinvention splits critics over its rage
content.standfirst: Mike Flanagan’s eight-part adaptation shifts Stephen King’s story into the social-media era and gives its characters more sympathetic histories. Critics disagree on whether that creates richer drama or takes the teeth out of Carrie’s revenge.

image.caption: Summer H Howell as Carrie in Mike Flanagan’s adaptation.

sources.originalTitle: Carrie review – the teenage hell-raiser’s glorious return couldn’t come at a better time
Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people
Cruel torment, depraved violence, evil turns: where did TV’s real baddies go?
The Carrie remake made me furious

segments.body: The new series begins after a school fire and works backward to Carrie White’s arrival at high school. Unlike earlier versions, she has been homeschooled, and her mother and classmates are given more context than in the novel. The bullying spreads through phones and social media, while the story also spends time on the people around Carrie.

perspectives.body: The i critic argues that the series removes the anger and agency that made King’s Carrie compelling, recasting her as a frightened figure while softening her mother and tormentors.

segments.title: Reinvention or defanging?
segments.body: The Guardian review welcomes the expanded character work, calling the series an intelligent coming-of-age drama as well as horror. The BBC’s advance discussion notes debate over Carrie’s appearance and her departure from the book, but says the show modernises its themes. A separate Guardian essay argues that this sympathetic approach reflects a wider trend of giving television’s villains understandable backstories.

perspectives.body: The Guardian review sees the series’ attention to Carrie’s family and classmates as a source of emotional richness, even as it makes the adaptation kinder than the original film.

content.headline: Bel honours Beldina Odenyo through the music her sister could not leave behind
content.shortHeadline: Bel keeps Beldina Odenyo’s music alive
content.standfirst: The documentary follows Leah McAleer as she tries to complete the album of her sister, the Kenyan-Scottish singer Beldina Odenyo, who died in 2021. It is also a portrait of an extraordinary voice shaped by trauma, racism and mental illness.

image.caption: Beldina Odenyo, whose music and life are the subject of the documentary Bel.

sources.originalTitle: Bel review – a tearful, heartbreaking tribute to a spellbinding singer

segments.body: Beldina Odenyo was 31 when she died, two weeks after a powerful performance at Edinburgh’s Usher Hall. In Bel, director Louise Lockwood draws on Odenyo’s songs and teenage video diaries, alongside interviews with people who knew her. Her sister Leah McAleer works to finish the music Odenyo left on her computer.

The film traces Odenyo’s childhood move from Kenya to Scotland and the racism and violence she experienced growing up. It also follows her mental-health struggles and the isolation that worsened during lockdown. McAleer calls completing the album a futile attempt to bring her sister back, but the documentary becomes a careful tribute to both Odenyo’s voice and their bond.

content.headline: Damilola: The Untold Story remembers the boy behind the national tragedy
content.shortHeadline: Damilola Taylor’s friends recall a loss that haunts them
content.standfirst: John Boyega and other childhood friends recall Damilola Taylor, who was murdered in 2000, and the fear and grief that followed. The documentary avoids true-crime spectacle to focus on the people who knew him and the memories they have carried into adulthood.

image.caption: Damilola Taylor, remembered by childhood friends in the documentary.

sources.originalTitle: Damilola: The Untold Story review – John Boyega’s trauma after losing his childhood friend is haunting

segments.body: Damilola Taylor was 10 when he was killed on his way home from a library in Peckham in 2000. This one-off documentary includes John Boyega and his sister Grace, who were among the last children to see him alive. They describe their fear and grief, while other friends remember Damilola as a cheerful newcomer to the estate.

The review praises the film for avoiding graphic reconstructions and familiar true-crime profiling. Instead, grainy home footage, stylised scenes and testimony from friends, the caretaker who found Damilola and a journalist who covered the case preserve the uncertainty and pain of memory. The documentary also resists reducing the North Peckham Estate to a stereotype.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans waiting for a return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future
content.standfirst: The BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special, and its co-production deal with Disney+ has ended without a replacement Doctor announced. Fans and former contributors reflect on the show’s history and the questions facing its next revival.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, from Christopher Eccleston to Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since Ncuti Gatwa’s departure, Doctor Who has been without a Doctor on screen. The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+ and cancelled a planned Christmas special; it is seeking another company to help fund future production, but none has yet stepped forward. The BBC declined interview requests for the article.

segments.title: A changing institution
segments.body: The feature traces the programme’s earlier cancellation and 2005 revival, then examines the changing showrunners, scripts and reactions to its recent casting. Contributors say its traditions of regeneration, kindness and curiosity have helped it endure, even as viewing figures fell and Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker faced abuse. The future remains unresolved.

perspectives.body: Lifelong fan Frank Skinner says the series did not need a major streaming investment simply to tell good stories, and urges the BBC to bring it back to television.

content.headline: Bake Off’s audience-choice week gives the tent a welcome shake-up
content.shortHeadline: Bake Off gets a sharper edge from its viewers
content.standfirst: Viewers set the challenges in the series’ first audience-choice week, bringing awkward family baking, improvised technicals and a wearable showstopper. The critic sees a welcome dose of unpredictability in a format whose cosy formula has grown stale.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood judge a Bake Off challenge.

sources.originalTitle: Bake Off is toughening up. Good

segments.body: For the first time, viewers rather than judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood set the Bake Off challenges. The bakers made cheesecake with family members, faced different technical bakes using basic ingredients and attempted wearable showstoppers. The week was not as chaotic as it might have been, but it loosened the programme’s usual rules.

The review argues that Bake Off’s gentle warmth once distinguished it from harsher reality television, but that the same cosiness now feels dated. The new format also gives Lawson and Hollywood more room to disagree, and allows the competition to show genuine mishaps without rushing to comfort contestants. The critic wants the show to keep that livelier balance.

content.headline: Ross Kemp’s paranoia puts the Faithful at risk on The Celebrity Traitors
content.shortHeadline: Ross Kemp’s nerves may hurt the Faithful
content.standfirst: The i’s episode analysis argues that Kemp’s habit of voicing every suspicion is giving the Traitors useful cover. His anxiety is spreading through the group, turning small gestures into possible clues and distracting the Faithful from more telling evidence.

image.caption: Ross Kemp competes on The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Ross Kemp’s Traitors paranoia will be the Faithfuls’ downfall

segments.body: On The Celebrity Traitors, Ross Kemp has mistaken ordinary gestures for possible murders and shared his suspicions aloud. The article contrasts his approach with a quieter strategy of observing and building a case, arguing that Kemp’s public anxiety makes him look more suspicious rather than safer.

The Traitors’ decision to leave Kemp above ground during a mission may make him appear to have been recruited, and his worries are already influencing other players’ theories. The analysis says the Faithful risk chasing accidental red herrings while overlooking stronger clues—and suggests Kemp should keep his suspicions to himself.

content.headline: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce revisit Daphne and Niles
content.shortHeadline: Frasier’s stars remember the slow-burn Daphne–Niles romance
content.standfirst: The actors look back on a seven-season sitcom courtship, from the tango in “Moon Dance” to the kiss that made the studio audience erupt. Their recollections also illuminate the friendship and careful comic timing behind the romance.

image.caption: Daphne and Niles in Frasier.

sources.originalTitle: ‘He was devastatingly sexy’: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on the love between Daphne and Niles

segments.body: Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce remember how Daphne and Niles’ attraction became a running thread through Frasier. The characters’ differences made the crush funny, while Niles’s visible longing and Daphne’s disbelief let the writers sustain the tension for years. Both actors say the relationship worked because the audience understood what Niles felt before Daphne did.

segments.title: Timing the payoff
segments.body: The actors recall rehearsing the tango in “Moon Dance” together and the audience’s reaction when the pair finally kissed. They also praise the writers for knowing when to resolve the long wait and when to leave a moment unspoken. Off screen, Leeves and Hyde Pierce remained close friends, a bond that informs their warm account of the series.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family to a familiar legal-drama world
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up gives its divorce drama a new family
content.standfirst: The spin-off moves the family-law setting of The Split to Manchester and centres a British Asian firm. Its cast and creative team say the aim is to keep the glossy relationship drama while letting a wider range of characters live ordinary, complicated lives.

image.caption: Ritu Arya leads The Split Up, overseen by executive producer Abi Morgan.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows barrister Aria Kishan, played by Ritu Arya, as she expects to inherit her father Dhruv’s Manchester law firm. After her mother’s death, he changes his succession plans, and a former romantic partner joins the firm. As in The Split, divorce cases and family tensions run alongside one another.

segments.title: Representation beyond the premise
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to create British Asian characters living recognisable lives, rather than making them represent every part of a culture. Executive producer Abi Morgan describes the series as an evolution of The Split’s focus on love, family, ambition and betrayal, with women working across its creative team.

perspectives.body: Ritu Arya says her casting alongside Sanjeev Bhaskar felt full-circle after growing up performing a home-made version of Goodness Gracious Me, a show she says helped her imagine a place for British Asian lives on television.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 delivers thrilling dogfights and a surprisingly moving story
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 fulfils the Top Gun fantasy
content.standfirst: The latest entry pairs spectacular aerial combat with a story that gives its pilots greater emotional presence than before. Its missions can become confusing amid visual clutter, but the review finds the flight, spectacle and drama add up to a series high point.

image.caption: A fighter jet in Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 casts the player as a supposed ace pilot whose reputation began as wartime propaganda. Dogfights, bombing runs and escort missions build on the series’ accessible flying, with a more complex control scheme for experienced players. The review praises the sense of speed and the way each mission creates high-pressure moments in the air.

The game’s story gets a larger role through animated first-person sequences and cinematic scenes that bring the player’s wing-mates to life. The review notes that some dialogue is clumsy and that cockpit battles can be hard to read, but finds the mix of character drama, music and aerial action unexpectedly moving. Online multiplayer could not be assessed during the review period.

content.headline: Resident Evil’s new film recreates the feeling of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil turns game mechanics into film language
content.standfirst: Zach Cregger’s adaptation leaves familiar heroes off screen and follows an ordinary courier through an escalating outbreak. The feature argues that its empty spaces, scarce ammunition and encounters with non-player characters capture the games’ uneasy rhythms.

image.caption: Director Zach Cregger and actor Austin Abrams on the Resident Evil film set.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: The film follows courier Bryan Hodukavich through a virus outbreak in Raccoon City. Rather than centre familiar characters such as Leon or Claire, it recreates the games’ structure: a vulnerable protagonist, locations that grow more threatening, weapons found along the way and too little ammunition to feel safe.

The article points to found recordings, terse conversations with other characters and the familiar sequence of a farmhouse, tunnel, hospital and sewer as ways the film borrows from play rather than simply translating plot. It argues that this approach makes the audience feel like a player gradually learning the rules of an unfamiliar horror world.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day has excellent combat and too little else
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day is let down by repetition
content.standfirst: The prequel delivers the series’ most satisfying combat, with destructible environments and fluid movement. But repetitive routes, collectibles and clumsy exploration rules make its campaign feel stretched beyond its strongest ideas.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day follows Marcus Fenix and his squad as the alien invasion begins. The review says the opening recaptures the horror and grit of the early Gears games, while the combat feels better than ever: movement is more fluid, cover feels natural and battles leave the environment visibly damaged.

The campaign repeatedly sends the squad across the same ruined city, with levels revisited and long stretches of open space filled with collectibles. Exploration can be punished by mission boundaries, despite the game encouraging players to search. The review concludes that the series’ signature combat remains strong, but the surrounding campaign rarely develops its ideas.

content.headline: How Roblox phishing scams trick children into handing over Robux
content.shortHeadline: The Roblox scam promising children free Robux
content.standfirst: Fake login pages offer players free in-game currency, then capture account details and sometimes authentication codes. Security specialists advise children to open Roblox through its official app or website rather than links sent in videos or chats.

image.caption: Roblox advises users not to follow links or download files from unknown senders.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children

segments.body: Fraudsters are using fake Roblox login pages to steal players’ usernames, passwords and virtual currency. Links may appear in YouTube or TikTok comments or Discord chats, promising free Robux and urging children to act quickly. The page can redirect users to the real Roblox site after harvesting their details, leaving little sign of what happened.

segments.title: Protecting an account
segments.body: NordVPN researchers say they found almost 200 addresses offering ready-made phishing pages over a seven-day period. Security experts advise opening Roblox directly through its official app or website and treating two-factor and backup codes like passwords. Roblox says account recovery is not guaranteed, though it may help in very limited circumstances.

content.headline: Playing Call of Duty with his adult son brings a father back to the game
content.shortHeadline: A father and son reconnect through Call of Duty
content.standfirst: A father revisits the co-op missions he once played with his five-year-old son, now 22. Their renewed teamwork turns a familiar shooter into a joyful record of time spent together—and an unexpectedly emotional farewell before they move to different parts of the world.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game a father and son revisit together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his son return to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the first game they played together when the boy was five. The missions that once defeated them now reward a different kind of teamwork: the cautious father scouts ahead while his son moves quickly through the level.

After repeated failures, they adapt their styles and finally complete the old missions. The writer describes the pleasure of playing without the guilt and responsibilities that can make gaming feel like another task. With both due to move to different parts of the world, his son says he will remember these sessions as some of their best times together.

content.headline: The volunteer Pokémon professors who keep competitive play running
content.shortHeadline: Meet Pokémon’s volunteer tournament professors
content.standfirst: At the 2026 world championships, volunteer Pokémon professors taught players, judged matches and helped keep the venue safe. Their work sustains competitive events, though the company declined to provide an official account of how all professors are compensated.

image.caption: Players gather at the 2026 Pokémon world championships in San Francisco.

sources.originalTitle: Meet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling

segments.body: Around 300 Pokémon professors were present at the 2026 world championships in San Francisco, according to the Pokémon Company International. These volunteers help run events, teach newcomers and officiate competitions. Their duties range from technical support to resolving card-game rulings and making sure results are recorded correctly.

segments.title: Rules, care and compensation
segments.body: Head judge Gemma Byard says officials must enforce rules while managing upset competitors and keeping events safe. Evelyne de Groot describes the role as a form of customer service that helps players enjoy the game. Some interviewed professors described different forms of compensation, but the company declined to provide an official explanation of its arrangements.

perspectives.body: Byard says spectators may see only a single ruling, while judges are responsible for understanding the full circumstances before making a decision.

content.headline: The White House’s gaming-themed arcade turns play into political propaganda
content.shortHeadline: The White House arcade weaponises game nostalgia
content.standfirst: A collection of pixel-art mini-games riffs on familiar titles to promote the Trump administration’s messaging about immigration and politics. The critic argues that their crude humour is less persuasive than it is revealing about the political use of game culture.

image.caption: Build the Wall, a White House arcade game based on Tetris.

sources.originalTitle: The Trump White House’s fetish for gamer culture has moved up a level with new arcade

segments.body: The White House’s online arcade borrows the look and mechanics of familiar games. One version of Tetris asks players to build a wall at the southern border; another turns a Snake-like game into a patrol collecting migrants in orange jumpsuits. The article describes the games as deliberately dehumanising and part of a wider effort to appropriate gaming imagery for political messaging.

segments.title: More provocation than persuasion
segments.body: The critic calls the games mean-spirited and poorly made, and suspects they may have been created using AI. The article argues that they are designed more to provoke a reaction than to persuade new audiences, while warning that gaming’s potential as a political tool should not be ignored as governments move beyond posting memes to making games themselves.

perspectives.body: Games and politics writer George Osborn says gaming-coded posts have reached substantially more people than ordinary White House posts, and sees the arcade as an escalation from borrowing game culture to using the medium itself.

content.headline: Could romance in Grand Theft Auto VI count as cheating?
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s romance debate is about real relationships
